Custom

/KUS-tum/ — rhymes with autumn · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A custom is a traditional practice or way of behaving that a particular group of people follows.

Removing your shoes at the door is a custom in many homes.

Worked Example

In Japan, guests present beautifully wrapped gifts with both hands as a sign of respect—a custom that reflects the culture's emphasis on courtesy and formality.

Custom is far more precise than "habit" here. A habit is a personal routine; a custom is a shared practice embedded in a culture. The two hands, the wrapping, the symbolism—these matter because they're part of a group's tradition, not just an individual's choice.

How Custom Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

convention

convention: a widely accepted social rule

habit

habit: a personal action repeated almost automatically

practice

practice: a usual, established way of doing something

Antonyms

exception

exception: a one-time break from the usual practice

novelty

novelty: something new with no tradition behind it

How Strong Is It? — preference → habit → custom → convention

preference vs. custom

preference vs. custom: A preference is far weaker than a custom: a preference is just one person's private liking, while a custom is a practice a whole community expects and follows.

habit vs. custom

habit vs. custom: A habit is weaker than a custom — a habit belongs to one person and forms almost automatically, while a custom is shared across a group and passed down over time.

convention vs. custom

convention vs. custom: A convention is stronger and more official than a custom: a custom is a group's traditional way of behaving, while a convention is so widely accepted it works almost like a formal rule.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — custom (< Latin consuetudo)

Root — custom (< Latin consuetudo): settled habit, familiar practice — from consuescere, 'to become thoroughly accustomed' (the old prefix com- and root suescere are fossilized and folded into this single chip) (Latin, via Old French costume)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin consuescere meant 'to become thoroughly accustomed,' and its noun consuetudo — worn down through Old French costume — became custom: a way of behaving a group has grown so used to that it turns into tradition.

Use the root in a new word: accustom

Use the root in a new word: accustom: When you become accustomed to early mornings, they stop feeling strange — accustom shares custom's Latin root meaning 'to make something into a settled habit.'

Word Choice

neutral / conversational

Custom is the word for shared, traditional ways of behaving that a group maintains. It's more social and cultural than the personal word 'habit.' Use custom when the practice reflects group identity or tradition; use habit for individual routines.
